english: Consider $n$ points in a plane, $n\ge4$, no three of which are collinear, and draw the $\binom{n}{2}$ lines each joining two of these points. Assume that no two of these lines are parallel and that no three of them pass through a common point other than one of the $n$ given points. Two of these lines are chosen at random. It is given that the probability that their point of intersection is not one of the $n$ given points is $\dfrac{7}{11}$. Then the number of points of intersection of these lines, other than the $n$ given points, is ______.
hindi: एक तल में $n$ बिन्दुओं ($n\ge4$) पर विचार कीजिए, जिनमें से कोई तीन संरेख नहीं हैं, तथा इनमें से दो-दो बिन्दुओं को मिलाने वाली $\binom{n}{2}$ रेखाएँ खींचिए। मान लीजिए कि इन रेखाओं में से कोई दो समान्तर नहीं हैं तथा $n$ दिए गए बिन्दुओं के अतिरिक्त किसी अन्य बिन्दु से इनमें से कोई तीन रेखाएँ नहीं गुज़रतीं। इन रेखाओं में से दो रेखाएँ यादृच्छया चुनी जाती हैं। दिया है कि उनका प्रतिच्छेदन बिन्दु $n$ दिए गए बिन्दुओं में से कोई न होने की प्रायिकता $\dfrac{7}{11}$ है। तब इन रेखाओं के, $n$ दिए गए बिन्दुओं के अतिरिक्त, प्रतिच्छेदन बिन्दुओं की संख्या ______ है।
solution: Two lines meet at a given point iff they share a point: $n\binom{n-1}{2}=\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$ pairs, so $P(\text{meet at a given point})=\dfrac{4}{n+1}$
Other intersection points: pairs not sharing a point, each giving a distinct point (no three concurrent): $\binom{45}{2}-10\binom{9}{2}=990-360=630$
solution_full: Lines from $n$ points with no three collinear: $L=\binom{n}{2}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, and the number of pairs of lines is $\binom{L}{2}=\dfrac{L(L-1)}{2}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\cdot\dfrac{n^{2}-n-2}{4}=\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)}{8}$.

Two distinct lines (not parallel) meet in exactly one point. Their intersection is a given point exactly when the two lines have a given point in common. For each of the $n$ points, the lines through it are the $n-1$ lines joining it to the others, giving $\binom{n-1}{2}$ pairs; two distinct lines share at most one given point, so there is no double counting: $n\binom{n-1}{2}=\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$ pairs.
So $P(\text{intersection is a given point})=\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)/2}{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)/8}=\dfrac{4}{n+1}$, and by the complement rule $P(\text{not a given point})=\dfrac{n-3}{n+1}$.

For $n=10$: $L=45$ lines and $\binom{45}{2}=990$ pairs, of which $10\binom{9}{2}=360$ meet at given points. The other $630$ pairs meet at points other than the given ones, and since no three lines are concurrent there, different pairs give different points. (Check: every $4$ of the points give $3$ such points, $3\binom{10}{4}=630$.)
originality_note: New: the probability that two random lines of a complete point configuration meet at one of the given points simplifies to 4/(n+1); its complement determines n and then the number of new intersection points (way 4: a hidden clean formula). Closest known: 'number of points of intersection of lines joining n points' and 'probability that a triangle has a side common with the polygon'. Different because: n is unknown and is found from a probability over pairs of lines, which needs the complement count of concurrent pairs.
